newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Jefferson Smurfit cautiously optimistic on future.
newsitem.headline: Jefferson Smurfit cautiously optimistic on future.

text.p: Paper and packaging giant Jefferson Smurfit Plc said on Tuesday that it was cautiously optimistic about the future but admitted it was unsure whether prices in the industry had bottomed out.

"What we have been through has been a very aggressive destocking phase and then a rebound which has been inevitable ... but we are not clear if what is now happening is the tail end of a destocking phase or the reestablishment of a pattern of growth and demand," Smurfit finance director Ray Curran told Reuters. "As a consequence we are cautious."
Smurfit, the world's leading producer of corrugated packaging materials, earlier reported a drop of 37 percent in first half pre-tax profit to 126 million Irish pounds ($203.7 million).
Curran said supply/demand imbalance continued to be fragile and the industry had taken a lot of downtime, particularly in the U.S.

"Linerboard pricing in the U.S. has seen further decline and transaction levels at the moment are in the $320-$340 range per U.S. tonne. So that is a further decline of $10-$15 from where were at the end of quarter two," he said.
Asked if prices could drop to the $290 per tonne, the floor during the previous cycle, Curran said that while he hoped not it was difficult to call at this stage.

"You can never say never but our view would be that things have possibly bottomed although we could be wrong," Curran said, adding that he was not very optimistic about a mooted price increase in September coming through.

"We have been pretty consistent in saying that we saw the real turn coming probably anytime between the third quarter of 1996 and the third quarter of 1997. That is a real wide gap but we do think it is a function of demand from the offshore side, specifically the Far East, that will drive the timing of the supply/demand rebalance."
Curran said there was no demand problem with the containerboard sector. It was a supply side problem.
"When people are in expectation of price increases they build inventories pretty aggressively but the reverse is also true and when they think prices will go down they aggressively destock," he said.

"That causes a tremendous distortion in the true underlying demand pattern. You get a huge surge in demand when they think things are going up and a huge dip in demand when they think things are going down," he said.
Curran said Smurfit has continually said that if the industry would learn to build machines to meet existing demand and not build machines to meet anticipated demand it would not have a problem.
"Clearly every new tonne that comes into capacity weakens the pricing structure. If you want to increase market share, buy someone with market share."
Curran said Smurfit had a healthy balance sheet and capital expenditure was being strictly controlled.
"We undoubtedly have one of the strongest balance sheets in the business. We have 830 million Irish pounds in cash, a gearing of something like 35 percent and very strong net worth," he said.
